strengths: The paper targets an important and practically useful problem: single-image 3D head reconstruction under severe viewpoint ambiguity, together with disentangled geometry/style editing. The ViT-to-Gaussian-Splatting design is coherent and supports both reconstruction and fine-tuned editing in one framework.

The main technical contribution, perceptual supervision from frozen DINOv2 and SAM 2.1 features, is well motivated. Using intermediate class/patch tokens rather than only pixel, L1, SSIM, or LPIPS losses gives semantic and high-frequency gradients. The ablations support this: on extreme Ava-256 views, the full loss improves DreamSim from 0.115 to 0.106 and ArcFace distance from 0.300 to 0.282 relative to LPIPS+L1, while the supplementary early-epoch analysis shows faster recovery of glasses, hair, and teeth.

Reconstruction results are strong on the reported benchmarks. In Table 1, the method ranks first in PSNR, LPIPS, DreamSim, and ArcFace on both Ava-256 settings, with particularly large gains on extreme views (15.9 PSNR and 0.282 ArcFace versus 14.2 and 0.416 for the strongest listed baseline in those respective metrics). Supplementary Tables 3 and 4 show similar trends on held-out NeRSemble identities and against FaceLift.

The paper emphasizes and empirically tests difficult side and opposing views, where several recent baselines exhibit geometric collapse or identity drift. The frontal- and side-input multi-angle comparisons, video-frame results, and out-of-distribution examples provide qualitative evidence of improved 3D consistency and robustness.

The editing extension is useful: FaRL segmentation maps control geometry while CLIP text features or reference-image features control style, enabling zero-shot prompt-based edits and an interactive GUI. The style/geometry matrix and prompt results demonstrate a compelling application layer.

The evaluation includes useful ablations on training data, individual losses, DINOv2 layers, patch versus class supervision, SHP-CNN, lightweight models, computational cost, and robustness. Training schedules, datasets, test subject IDs, preprocessing choices, GPU requirements, and timing are also supplied in the supplementary material.
The authors state that training/inference code and the GUI will be released, which would improve reproducibility and make the system practically usable.
weaknesses: Material: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental. The reconstruction pipeline builds directly on the LAM ViT-to-Gaussian design, including the additional trained ViT branch, cross-attention 3D decoder, and Gaussian-latent generation. The principal new ingredient is the DINOv2/SAM 2.1 feature-loss combination and training recipe; although effective, the representation itself is not a major departure from prior transformer-based Gaussian head models.

Material: Equation (7) defines the final objective as a product, L = lambda_D L_D * lambda_S L_S, rather than the usual weighted sum. If this is literal, it has unusual optimization consequences: the objective and gradients can vanish when either term is small, and the two losses no longer contribute independently. This needs justification or correction to a sum; as written it is a technical ambiguity.

Material: The claim of end-to-end 3D consistency is complicated by SHP-CNN, a per-image 2D sharpening network applied after Gaussian rasterization. A view-wise post-processor can introduce cross-view or temporal inconsistencies, and the paper itself reports flickering. The ablations mainly measure aggregate image metrics; there is no explicit multi-view feature-consistency, geometry, depth, or temporal-consistency evaluation isolating this module.

Material: The editing contribution is evaluated almost entirely qualitatively. There are no quantitative measures of geometry preservation across styles, identity retention, text-image/CLIP alignment, disentanglement, or edit accuracy, and no user study. The comparison to NeRFFaceEditing is limited to a visual demo subject. Thus the strong claims about advanced 3D editing are less rigorously supported than the reconstruction claims.

Material: Quantitative evaluation breadth is limited. The supplementary material lists only 11 Ava-256 identities and 5 held-out NeRSemble identities for the main reconstruction benchmarks, despite many rendered views. Additional in-the-wild and generated-input robustness is shown through curated figures rather than a standardized benchmark. Statistical significance or variance across identities is also not reported.

Material: Some architecture and training details needed for full reproducibility are missing or underspecified, including the exact appearance representation (RGB versus spherical harmonics), rendering resolution, camera/view sampling details, Gaussian regularization, and how a single global CLIP embedding is injected into per-patch decoder features for editing. The editing fine-tuning description, especially the phrase about inputting the same image twice into CLIP and FFHQ, is also unclear.

The phrase 'drop-in replacement for standard losses' is slightly overstated. In Table 2 the proposed full loss has the same PSNR and a worse LPIPS score than LPIPS+L1 (0.291 versus 0.285), although it improves DreamSim, ArcFace, and qualitative detail. Likewise, GAGAvatar achieves higher SSIM on novel NeRSemble and Ava-256 views. The gains are convincing but should be described as perceptual/identity and extreme-view improvements rather than uniform superiority.

Minor presentation issues should be corrected. In supplementary Table 5, the first numeric column is labeled SSIM but contains values such as 15.4 and 16.1, which are clearly PSNR-scale values. There are also typos such as 'mutli-view,' 'resutls,' and 'incl due,' and the paper would benefit from a clearer distinction between the static 3D Gaussian output and the post-processed sharpened image.

The acknowledged limitations—no expression transfer, no built-in temporal modeling, flickering on video, and baked illumination—are honest but materially constrain applications such as avatar animation and relighting.
